messages.body_plain:
If you're simply trying to have nimbleMCMC accomplish the same steps as the more explicit nimbleModel-buildMCMC-compileNimble-Cmcmc$run sequence that you did get to work, I think you need the first argument to nimbleMCMC to be nimble.fixed.s and also to include the same constants = constants argument you used for nimbleModel.  Alternatively it should work to give constants = c(constants, jags.onestate.data) and omit the data argument.

nimbleMCMC just manages the sequence of steps you've already done with some helpful management of chains and output.  You can get that management from the steps you did but with runMCMC(Cmcmc, <look at other arguments>) instead of Cmcmc$run().

Alternatively you can give nimbleMCMC "model = simple.model" and omit the constants, data, and inits, since they were provided when you created simple.model.  However, if you've already compiled simple.model from the first workflow, then you'll need to re-create simple.model for nimbleMCMC, so you might as well pass the code, constants, data and inits and let nimbleMCMC create the model.

nimbleMCMC will use check=TRUE by default, which can be slow can generate warnings or show messages about incomplete initialization.  If you want the same behavior are your direct use of nimbleModel, use check=FALSE again.  The first workflow always provides more control.

messages.subject: another WAIC question
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to specify "WAIC=TRUE" in the call to "buildMCMC" (or to "configureMCMC") for a simple model, and I keep getting an error message that one of the data nodes has un-monitored upstream parameters. This is the case, even when I specify all  parameters to monitor, or when I provide
 "monitors = model$getNodeNames(stochOnly = TRUE, includeData = FALSE)" as suggested in this thread (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/nimble-users/waic$20question%7Csort:date/nimble-users/ONCGokjWIUs/8vGYt1paCwAJ).

The exact message I get is

Error in mcmc_checkWAICmonitors(model = model, monitors = sampledNodes,  :
  In order for a valid WAIC calculation, all parameters of data nodes in the model must be monitored, or be downstream from monitored nodes. See help(buildMCMC) for more information on valid sets of monitored nodes for WAIC calculations.
 Currently, the following data nodes have un-monitored upstream parameters:
 y[1]

Can anyone tell me what up-stream parameter needs to be monitored, and how I do that? I think it might have something to do with the fact that y[1] depends on N[1], which is supplied only as a prior, but if so, I'm not sure how to resolve it.

Example code is below.

Thanks,
Glenn

library(nimble)
R <- 0.05
n1 <- 20
J <- 35

N <- matrix(0,J,1)
N[1] <- n1
# project population
for(j in 2:J){
N[j] <- round(rnorm(1,N[j-1]*(1+R),0.1*N[j-1]))
}
plot(1:J,N)

# exponential model (allowing variable R)
modelExp <- nimbleCode({
# priors
N[1] ~ dnorm(20,sd=2)
R ~ dgamma(1,5)
sd.obs ~ dgamma(1,0.5)
# abundance model
for (j in 1:(J-1)) {
N[j+1] <- (1+R)*N[j]
}
# observation model
for (j in 1:J) {
y[j] ~ dnorm(N[j],sd=sd.obs)
}
})

# specify MCMC controls for nimble
ni <- 1000
nt <- 4
nb <- 1000
nc <- 3

# exponential
nConsts <- list(J=J)
nData <- list(y=as.vector(N))
nInits <- list(R=0.25,sd.obs=2,N=c(20,rep(NA,J-1)))
parameters <- c("N","R","sd.obs")

nim <- nimbleModel(code=modelExp,name='nim',constants=nConsts,data=nData,inits=nInits)
nimMCconf <- configureMCMC(nim,monitors=parameters,thin=nt,useConjugacy = FALSE)
nimMC <- buildMCMC(nimMCconf,enableWAIC = TRUE)
Cnim <- compileNimble(nim)

messages.body_plain:
Hey all,

I've been using NIMBLE to implement a discrete-time Poisson Hidden Markov Model, but am having convergence issues with the lambda parameters. I have tried RW, conjugate, and blocking samplers for these parameters, both a poisson and zero inflated poisson distribution for the data, thinning, as well as some fist shaking at the computer. Any help/further suggestions would be greatly appreciated.

I'm including a brief model overview below, and have attached NIMBLE code and simulated latent state values for reproducibility. In the code I am holding the latent states as constants to try and isolate the issues with the lambda convergence, but ultimately these will be estimated as well.

Cheers,
Meridith

2-state Penalized HMM Model  (see attached for NIMBLE model code)

Observed Data:
Y_t ~ Poisson(lambda_{X_t})

Augmented Data Scheme:
Y_t = Y_Low + Y_Diff * I{X_t = H}

Y_L ~ Pois(lambda_{X_t = L})
Y_Diff ~ Pois(lambda_{X_t = H})

Lambda Priors:
lambda_{X_t = L} ~ Gamma(shape = .005, rate = .7)
lambda_{X_t = H} ~ Gamma(shape = .05, rate = .7)

Latent States:
X_t ~ Mult(1, P_{X_{t-1}}) (Bernulloi in commented out code due to 2-states, but generalized to Mult)

Probability Transition Matrix Priors
 P[i, ] ~ Dirch(alpha = theta[i, ] )

where theta provides a penalty tuning parameter.

theta = [tau, 1
              1, tau]

where a larger tau value places more weight on staying in a latent state for a longer period of time before switching (i.e. from Low to High or vic versa).

I'm not seeing where there are data values to inform any parameters.

It looks like both y_l and y_diff are not given as data, so they are being sampled as well.  In effect it looks like lambda_l will follow its prior but in a slow way because of the many y_l[t]'s also being sampled as if they are posterior predictive nodes.  You could use monitors2 and thin2 to get a thinner sample of y_l and y_diff and try to understand what is happening.  I think it is an mcmc phenomenon, not a nimble problem.

When I do model$setData('y_l') after the model$simulate(c("y_l", "y_diff"), then y_l is now data and I get a sensible well-mixed posterior for lambda_l centered around its correct (simulation) value of 0.007.  I did not do a similar experiment with y_diff and lambda_diff.

HTH.
-Perry

messages.subject: Re: Question about the random index in a loop function

messages.body_plain:
That's somewhat tricky.  K definitely can't go in the index range of the for loop.  I think you could take whatever is inside the for loop and use new nimbleFunctions (for deterministic or stochastic nodes) that also take K as an argument and decide what to do according to K.  You could either convert scalar declarations into a single vector declaration that uses K as an argument.  Or you could keep scalar declarations but provide i and K as arguments and only do calculations if i < K.  Or some other arrangement along similar lines.  If that doesn't help, can you send more detail on the problem?

messages.body_plain:
The additional detail is helpful.  I suggest looking in our User Manual on how to write user-defined distributions.  You could write say dCustomDirichlet that takes K as a parameter.  You would then use

pi[1:maxK] ~ dCustomDirichlet(gamma[1:lengthGamma], K)

Inside dCustomDirichlet, you would use only the 1:K portion of pi[1:maxK] (which will be called x inside dCustomDirichlet), and whatever portion of gamma you need.

I think having K as a stochastic index in the categorical will work, but if not, you can also write a custom version of this distribution to do what you need.

Note that, if the dimensions of gamma are stochastic, then the dimensions not currently involved in the Dirichlet calculation for pi (due to a possibly small value of K) will follow their prior, which may or may not make it easy for a larger K to be accepted.

Here is a more involved approach.  We have been doing some work on reversible-jump-like samplers.  I include the "-like" because technically the dimension of the model object does not change, the but the dimensions of what we use at different times does change.  In your case, I think one could write a sampler that uses reversible-jump logic when K changes.  You could look at how the RJ samplers for variable inclusion in version 0.8.0 work for ideas.

-Perry

P.S. What I meant about i < K was that this condition could be used inside a nimbleFunction providing a custom distribution.

> The additional detail is helpful.  I suggest looking in our User Manual on how to write user-defined distributions.  You could write say dCustomDirichlet that takes K as a parameter.  You would then use
>
> pi[1:maxK] ~ dCustomDirichlet(gamma[1:lengthGamma], K)
>
> Inside dCustomDirichlet, you would use only the 1:K portion of pi[1:maxK] (which will be called x inside dCustomDirichlet), and whatever portion of gamma you need.
>
> I think having K as a stochastic index in the categorical will work, but if not, you can also write a custom version of this distribution to do what you need.
>
> Note that, if the dimensions of gamma are stochastic, then the dimensions not currently involved in the Dirichlet calculation for pi (due to a possibly small value of K) will follow their prior, which may or may not make it easy for a larger K to be accepted.
>
> Here is a more involved approach.  We have been doing some work on reversible-jump-like samplers.  I include the "-like" because technically the dimension of the model object does not change, the but the dimensions of what we use at different times does change.  In your case, I think one could write a sampler that uses reversible-jump logic when K changes.  You could look at how the RJ samplers for variable inclusion in version 0.8.0 work for ideas.
>
> -Perry
